USENIX Association                           20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation                   1669
though they must not be linearized before [35]. We omit
describing readNext and prefixTrim for lack of space.
   Optimizing checkTail: The protocol described above
can be inefficient since weakTail requires accessing cloud
storage. We can drastically reduce the common-case cost
and latency of checkTail by using a fast-path checkTail that
goes to the sequencer rather than the LogDrive. We only
use the weakTail on the LogDrive as a slow-path once
the log is sealed. If the sequencer is unavailable, we first
seal the log; and then switch to the slow-path.
   We do have to be careful in this case to avoid having two
sources of truth for the tail. For example, a slow-path re-
sponse might see a tail 𝑋 on the LogDrive; but a subsequent,
non-overlapping fast-path checkTail invocation can return
𝑋 − 1 as the tail, resulting in a linearizability violation (for
example, if the writer of entry 𝑋 − 1 went to sleep after
writing to the LogDrive but before calling completeSlot on
                                                                          Figure 6. SMR via LogDrives: each SMR-replicated server
the sequencer).
                                                                          stores all its hard state in cloud storage. Servers do not interact
   To avoid such linearizability violations, the checkTail uses
                                                                          via RPCs at any layer, with the exception of the soft-state se-
the fast-path sequencer-based tail check before accessing the
                                                                          quencer in the AtomicLog.
seal bit; if the seal bit is set, the client retries the tail check
on the slow-path. As a result, once the seal bit is set, all
subsequently linearized checkTail operations return values
from the slow-path.                                                       4.1   Discussion

5.3    Conflux in K2
As noted earlier, Conflux is a general-purpose SMR system
that can replicate any deterministic service with an arbitrary
API. To support K2, we implement a particular service called
the K2MetaStore. In the remainder of this discussion, we
use Conflux interchangeably with K2MetaStore (until we
introduce other APIs). Figure 7 shows the subset of this API
used in the critical path of publish-subscribe requests.
   For each topic, Conflux stores an ordered list of pointers
called DataRefs. To a first approximation, a DataRef is a
pointer to some external piece of data. Accordingly, when a
broker stores data in S3, it creates an S3DataRef – a pointer           Figure 8. K2 servers store data blobs in cloud storage and

8   Related Work
                                                                       Integrating versioning and timelock checks into SSD
This paper is the first to propose a versioning system while us-    firmware makes versioning and timelock policies less flexible,
ing a storage device that forbids overwrites for a fixed period.    thereby restricting their use cases. By excluding versioning
TD constructs a secure backup solution on top of an isolated        from the TCB, our approach enables easy updates to version-
timelock primitive, which was not previously known to be            ing policies and optimizations in untrusted software, with-
possible. This is challenging as the timelock drive forbids all     out altering TCB code. As a result, TD enables several uses
overwrites, including metadata, for a fixed period. We also         beyond encryption ransomware, as detailed in Section 3.5.
formally verify the security guarantees of TD.                      Commercial products, such as ExaGrid and Oracle, imple-
   Backups and Versioning. The traditional ransomware de-           ment “retention timelocks” by enforcing retention periods in
fense is data backups. Common policies include version-             application- or service-level backup logic [12, 44]. In con-
ing [9, 14, 33], snapshotting [7], and delta backups [6, 8, 54].    trast, our solution timelocks physical blocks on disk. It isolates
These solutions are implemented in software and are thus            timelocks from versioning logic, resulting in a minimal TCB
vulnerable to common malware attacks that compromise the            that improves security and flexibility.
OS [18, 31], and are thus inadequate for ransomware defense.           Ransomware Detection and Prevention. Another line of
However, the versioning policies and optimizations they use         defense is ransomware detection, which monitors I/O and data
can be implemented in TD’s untrusted VS.                            patterns to flag malicious behavior [3, 28, 32]. But even when

introduced to reduce the total migration time and transferred      HPT manageability, cross-table consistency maintenance, and
data compared to the conventional pre-copy scheme. By di-          IOPT fault handling through three key techniques: (1) lock-
rectly switching the VM to the target host and lazily transfer-    reduced parallelism for dirty page registration, which reduces
ring all remaining memory data, post-copy effectively elim-        total downtime by up to 47.0%; (2) a decoupled userfault han-
inates the pre-copy convergence problem [31, 52]. In con-          dling pipeline based on parallel data copying with a separate
trast, other optimized pre-copy approaches (e.g., compres-         PVA and mixed page table updates, which reduces PCT by
sion [27, 53] and CPU throttling [42]) can only mitigate,          89.6% and improves guest performance by up to 4.1×; and
rather than eliminate, the convergence problem while simulta-      (3) identification and pre-transmission of pass-through device
neously introducing host resource over-consumption or nega-        states, which eliminates up to 98.5% of IOPFs.
tively impacting guest performance.                                   The design principles of M3U are fully generalizable to

E    Porting LibVMI to Firecracker
LibVMI relies on the KVM-VMI project to provide general-
purpose introspection capabilities. KVM-VMI is an extension
of KVM that enables fine-grained introspection mechanisms.
To perform introspection, LibVMI communicates with KVM
(over the KVMI extension) through a dedicated socket.
   Figure 7 illustrates how we integrated LibVMI with Fire-
cracker. When a VMI application starts, it invokes the Lib-
VMI initialization function, which connects to the VMM and
requests the creation of an introspection socket ( 1 ). With
QEMU, LibVMI relies on libvirt’s qemu driver for this step;
however, to the best of our knowledge, no libvirt plugin exists
for Firecracker. To overcome this limitation, we extended the
Firecracker API to allow introspection-socket creation via
HTTP requests. We also implemented a LibVMI Firecracker
driver to handle (dis)connection with Firecracker.
   Once the socket is created, LibVMI calls a libkvmi func-
tion to connect to the VMM introspection socket ( 2 ). The
KVMI protocol performs a three-step handshake to establish

of hundreds of threads [6]. To the scheduler, these threads             4     Design of V BOID S
are independent actors; CFS has no structural concept of a
“container” as an executable unit and cannot naturally enforce          The design goal of V BOID S is to address the fundamen-
concurrency bounds – it cannot dynamically limit a container            tal mismatch between the massive thread-level concurrency
to executing on exactly N cores simultaneously (only static             exposed by containers and the much coarser physical paral-
pinning), nor can it prevent the “split-brain” scattering of a          lelism of modern multicore hardware. Our design is guided
container’s threads across disjoint cores or NUMA nodes.                by three principles: (1) Restore placement stability through
                                                                        coarse granularity: The root cause of scheduling chaos is
                                                                        that containers expose too many independent migration can-
Task groups. In the Linux kernel, the abstract concept of a             didates. Restoring locality requires substantially reducing the
container is materialized as a task_groups (cgroups [6]).               scheduler’s decision space with coarser-grained placement.
Container runtimes like Docker [1] map each container to                (2) Minimize hot-path interference: The Linux scheduler’s
a distinct task_groups. The task_groups aggregates the                  hot path must remain fast and wait-free; any design that in-

transparent, drop-in nature of the standard kernel scheduler,
while introducing schemes to mitigate scheduling chaos.                 We presented V BOID S, a container scheduling system that
Lightweight virtualization. Micro-VMs, such as Firecracker              restores stability to high-density container deployments by
[10] and Kata Containers [4] address multi-tenancy by en-               raising the scheduler’s placement granularity from individual
forcing strong isolation boundaries [3, 4, 10, 12, 25, 33, 40, 47].     threads to B OIDS. By introducing B OIDS as container-level
They expose a fixed set of vCPUs to the host scheduler, rather          virtual scheduling units, V BOID S decouples thread-level exe-
than all guest processes/threads, which naturally mitigates             cution from host-level placement, allowing the kernel to make
scheduling chaos and stabilizes load balancing. However,                fewer, more stable, and more locality-preserving scheduling
they also introduce full virtualization overhead and reduce             decisions. V BOID S combines this coarse-grained abstraction
flexibility in resource over-subscription. V BOID S effectively         with a two-level balancing mechanism. The inter-core bal-
extends the vCPU abstraction to native containers, providing            ancer migrates B OIDS as aggregate units to reduce global im-
the stability of a vCPU without the performance penalty of              balance, while the intra-container balancer redistributes tasks
full virtualization or the rigidity of fixed resource constraints.      across a container’s B OIDS to preserve work conservation and
                                                                        avoid internal hotspots. This design provides VM-like place-
8    Discussions                                                        ment stability without requiring full virtualization, manual
                                                                        pinning, or rigid CPU partitioning, meanwhile preserving the
V BOID S bridges the gap between spatial partitioning (pin-
                                                                        flexibility and efficiency of containers that are attractive for
ning) and temporal throttling (CFS quotas). V BOID S adopts
                                                                        cloud-native deployment. Our evaluation shows that V BOID S
spatial concurrency bounding – by mapping threads onto a
                                                                        substantially reduces migration-induced locality disruption
fixed set of migratable B OIDS, it bounds a container’s par-
                                                                        and improves end-to-end performance for chaos-prone mi-
allelism – while preserving temporal flexibility through a
                                                                        croservice workloads. V BOID S’s abstraction provides a prac-
two-level scheduling hierarchy. This provides pinning-like
                                                                        tical foundation for future adaptive policies, including dy-
isolation benefits and quota-like fairness benefits.
                                                                        namic B OID provisioning and user-extensible scheduling.
   However, short-lived microservices that rely on rapid fork-
ing pose unique placement challenges. Placing child threads             10    Acknowledgments

Figure 6: The Overview of ADAngel. In contrast to traditional static approaches, namely llama.cpp (which incurs hardware
resource waste due to weight upcasting) and ABQ-LLM (which hits a shared memory wall during prefill due to bit-disaggregation,
detailed in Section 6.2), ADAngel is built upon the ❶ DPR Computation Model. By analyzing hardware architecture, ADAngel
constructs a ❷ Computation Strategy Set based on DPR constructs and employs a ❸ Strategy Dispatcher to map each mpGEMM
task to the optimal computation strategy during APQ LLM inference. As indicated by the dashed paths (offline stage), ADAngel
designs the strategy set under DPR guidance and evaluates these strategies on the target LLM to generate a dispatch table. As
indicated by the solid arrows (runtime stage), ADAngel (a) retrieves the appropriate strategy based on the problem size and
bit-width of the mpGEMM task, and (b) invokes the corresponding kernel to complete the computation.

Figure 10 shows the impact of temporal reuse across GEMM
shapes. Temporal reuse buffers tiles locally so the same A
or B tiles are reused across iterations instead of repeatedly
loaded from DRAM.
   We compare TileLoom with and without temporal reuse
over different M and N values. As with spatial reuse, this opti-
mization is most useful in memory-bound regimes, so we de-
crease K as M and N grow to keep the configurations memory-
bound. In this setting, temporal reuse yields speedups up
to 1.12×. The benefit increases with M and N, since larger
dimensions create more opportunities to reuse the same A           Figure 11: Validation of TileLoom’s performance model
or B tiles. Thus, temporal reuse is most helpful when M or         against measured GEMM performance.

                            Abstract                              ers [15, 36, 41]. However, this kernel-per-operator execution
We introduce Mirage Persistent Kernel (MPK), the first com-       model limits several key cross-operator GPU optimizations.
piler and runtime system that automatically transforms multi-        First, modern GPUs impose an implicit kernel barrier be-
GPU model inference into a single high-performance mega-          tween consecutive launches on the same stream to ensure
kernel. MPK introduces an SM-level graph representation           that all threads from the previous kernel complete before
that captures data dependencies at the granularity of individ-    any thread from the next kernel begins. While this mecha-
ual streaming multiprocessors (SMs), enabling cross-operator      nism correctly enforces data dependencies, it prevents cross-
software pipelining, fine-grained overlap of computation and      operator software pipelining and forces dependent operators
communication, and other optimizations that are infeasible        to execute strictly sequentially. NVIDIA recently introduced
under the conventional kernel-per-operator execution model.       programmatic dependent launch (PDL) [11], which allows

all operators into one kernel, they enable cross-operator soft-             over task execution and scheduling without additional kernel
ware pipelining, allowing data for the next operator to be                  launches during model execution. To achieve this goal, the
prefetched while computation for the current operator is still              runtime partitions a GPU’s SMs into workers and schedulers.
in progress. Third, they support fine-grained overlap of com-               Each worker maintains a dedicated task queue and executes

execution that more effectively hides communication latency.                track dependencies across tasks and dispatch tasks once their

to automatically search for efficient kernel implementations
from high-level specifications [26, 38, 39, 42, 47]. However,      This paper presents MPK, the first compiler and runtime sys-

on manual design. For example, FlashDMoE fuses mixture-            of computation and communication, and the elimination of

deep GPU expertise, and they do not generalize across mod-         a single mega-kernel while preserving compatibility with

solution that automatically transforms a tensor program into a     high-performance, compiler-driven inference systems.

The artifact validates the paper’s main performance claims:
(i) on single-batch serving, MPK reduces per-token latency       All runs use offline batched inference with a fixed prompt
by 1.0–1.7× over vLLM and SGLang, with the largest gains         length of 64, 1024 decoded tokens, and greedy decoding;

(Figures 12 and 13).

Contents
The repository holds the MPK compiler and in-kernel run-
time, a runnable demo for each model under demo/, and one
evaluation driver per GPU under artifact_evaluation/.
A driver sweeps the five models over batch sizes 1 to 16 for
all four systems and writes one result file per run, recording
the system, GPU, model, batch size, and measured per-token
latency. Collecting these files reproduces Figure 9 and the
ablation figures. A setup.sh script installs the dependencies
and builds MPK.

Hosting
The artifact is on the frozen branch tgx-osdi26-ae of
https://github.com/mirage-project/mirage (commit
8b981a4), archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.
5281/zenodo.20563064 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20563064).

Requirements
Hardware. One NVIDIA A100, H100 (SXM), or B200 for
the single-GPU sweeps, and a multi-GPU node (4–8 H100s)
for the tensor-parallel experiments. The four smaller models
fit on a 40 GB A100; Qwen3-30B-A3B needs at least 80 GB
and runs on an 80 GB A100, an H100, or a B200.
Software. Linux with CUDA (12.8 in the paper), PyTorch 2.7,
NVSHMEM and OpenMPI for the multi-GPU runs, and
transformers 4.57.1. setup.sh installs these and builds
MPK; vLLM and SGLang each run in a separate virtual envi-
ronment.

Kernel orchestration is the process of mapping a compu-
tation graph to hardware-specific kernels [15]. This problem       Data movement optimizations have become extremely impor-
is commonly addressed by operator fusion [2, 3, 9, 23], which      tant in tensor compilers to achieve good performance. VTC is
fuses multiple operators into a single kernel, thereby elimi-      the first compilation framework to eliminate all unnecessary
nating data movements of intermediate results. However, this       data movement that spans across all data movement oper-
type of work cannot optimize data movement operators that          ators in a given tensor computational graph. We introduce
are hard to fuse with other operators. VTC takes a computa-        the concept of a virtual tensor that allows VTC to track data
tion graph after operator fusion as input and further eliminates   movement between different physical tensors without instanti-
data movements between fused kernels.                              ating intermediate tensors. VTC’s data movement elimination
                                                                   algorithm allows us to achieve superior performance on a

While continuation-centric computing can improve the per-           This paper presents continuation-centric computing, a new
formance of serverless-style run-to-completion functional           operating system design paradigm, and evaluates it with Arca,
workloads, it is not a good fit for all use cases. We identify      a research OS that provides continuation capture as a core
several categories of application which would be difficult to       service. By designing Arca around this primitive, we found

  StateObject API                             Semantics
  StartAction(header) → bool                  Start an atomic action, (optionally) receive the given libDSE message header. If returned
                                              false, the message originates from rolled back state and should be discarded.
  EndAction() → header                        End an atomic action and (optionally) produce a header that encodes dependencies for any
                                              outgoing messages resulting from this action.
  Connect(config)                             Connect this StateObject to a libDSE Coordinator using the given configuration. Must be
                                              invoked exactly once before performing any other operation.
  Refresh()                                   Refresh should be periodically called to perform libDSE background tasks and guarantee
                                              progress for the cluster.
  Detach() → sthread                          Temporarily suspend an action and produce a sthread that can be used for speculative
                                              operations independent of this StateObject.
  Merge(sthread) → bool                       Resume an action by merging the detached sthread back into this StateObject and update
                                              its dependencies. If false, the state leading to the creation of the sthread was rolled back
                                              and the sthread should be discarded.
  sthread API                                 Semantics
  Receive(header) → bool                      Attempt to receive the given libDSE message header. If returned false, the message should
                                              be discarded. Throws exception if the sthread is rolled back.
  Send() → header                             Produce a header that encodes current dependencies of this sthread.
  Barrier()                                   Blocks until all state observed by this sthread becomes non-speculative. Throws exception if
                                              the sthread is rolled back.
  StateObject Callbacks                       Semantics
  Persist(v, metadata, onPersist)             Persist the current state and metadata as version v and then invoke onPersist.
  Restore(v) → metadata                       Recover (or roll back) to the given version and return associated metadata.
  Prune(v)                                    Signal that a version (and all that precede it) can be pruned.
  ListVersions() → metadata[]                 List all unpruned versions and associated metadata.

   Finally, sthreads support barriers, which provide fine-

ceived becomes non-speculative, thus preventing speculation
across the barrier. Only sthreads are allowed to invoke barri-

when interacting with external entities. For example, in line

of line 20 will be delayed until the response becomes non-

                                                                 Nixie manages memory at the granularity of CUDA-allocated
                                                                 chunk (i.e., the units returned by cudaMalloc). Each chunk
                                                                 may reside in one of four locations: (1) GPU memory, (2)
                                                                 CPU pinned memory, (3) CPU paged memory, or (4) disk.
                                                                 Unlike UVM, chunks placed in GPU memory do not require
                                                                 CPU pinned memory. To avoid fragmentation in CPU pinned
                                                                 memory or paged memory, we split a chunk into 2 MB blocks,
                                                                 where a block is the unit of data migration between locations.
                                                                    Nixie’s design follows two key principles. First, Nixie coor-
                                                                 dinates the control over both compute and memory allocation.
                                                                 When the scheduler selects an application to run, it proac-
                                                                 tively migrates that application’s chunks into GPU memory
                                                                 while simultaneously evicting other applications’ chunks to

The ML models selected for evaluation are targeted specif-
ically for the 32 GB RTX 5090. If a GPU with a different
VRAM capacity is used for evaluation, we suggest using mod-
els that fit into the GPU while maximizing VRAM usage, to
best reflect our settings.

2.4                                      Our Proposal and Design Goals

microkernel-based FPGA shell architecture. Inspired by the                                                                                                                                                 3.1       System Overview
microkernel concept [4, 68, 81, 89], 𝜇Shell enables the modular
deployment and execution of FPGA accelerators. Unlike the                                                                                                                                                  Figure 7 shows the overview of 𝜇Shell, comprised of guest

                                                                    Task scheduler. We implement 𝜇Shell’s component-aware

the number of state overlays over time, we believe that it        We present vBPF, a virtualization layer that adopts a late-
is acceptable in practice for three reasons. First, most dy-      binding execution model. Guided by the insight of dynamic
namic kernel states like sk_buff are short-lived, allowing        dispatch in polymorphic languages, vBPF resolves the fun-

A        MILP Formulation
Here, we present the MILP formulation of the preemptive
scheduling problem described in §4.2.
     Consider a set of tasks T = {τ1 , τ2 , · · · , τ|T | } submitted
to a cluster of M nodes G = {n1 , n2 , · · · , nM }, where each
node n j possesses S j GPUs. Each task is defined as a tuple
τi = ⟨wi , gi , ζi , ψi , ιi ⟩, requesting wi pods with gi GPUs each.
The task type is denoted by ζi ∈ {0, 1} (representing LP/spot
and HP, respectively), and the task includes D checkpoint
milestones ψi = {ci,1 , · · · , ci,D }.
     Additionally, let ιi = {⟨ti,1    s ,t e , f ⟩, · · · , ⟨t s ,t e , f
                                          i,1 i,1             i,Ei i,Ei i,Ei ⟩}
represent the set of Ei runtime logs for task τi . Each log cor-
responds to the k-th execution run, starting at ti,k             s , ending at
 e , and achieving the f -th checkpoint. The scheduler aims

to optimize the following dual objectives, formulated as a
mixed-integer linear programming problem over a discrete
time horizon t ∈ {1, . . . , T }:

of pods assigned to task τi on node n j at time t, and α is
a weighting factor. Constraint (2b) enforces physical GPU
limits per node. Constraint (2c) ensures gang-scheduling re-
quirements during each active run. Constraints (2d) and (2e)
enforce strict priority, restricting evictions and interruptions
to spot tasks only. Constraint (2f) correlates task duration
with completed checkpoints; by convention we set fi,0 ≜ 0
and ci,0 ≜ 0 so that the constraint is well-defined for k = 1.
Finally, Constraint (2g) restricts the decision variables to non-
negative integers.

2220    20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation                                      USENIX Association
C.3    Contents
The artifact includes the source code for all major components
of M IMESYS, including training data collection, diffusion-
model training, and execution-driven alignment. In addition,
it provides the scripts, configurations, and profiling infras-
tructure used to generate, execute, and evaluate the workload
mixes presented in the paper.
C.4    Hosting
The artifact is available at https://github.com/ldos-
project/mimesys. The artifact-eval branch contains
the version prepared for artifact evaluation.
C.5    Requirements
The artifact is designed to run on Linux systems capable
of executing stressors (e.g., Fleetbench and stress-ng) and
collecting resource-utilization profiles using TACC’s HPC
monitoring infrastructure. Training requires NVIDIA GPUs
with CUDA 12.x support. Detailed hardware and software
dependencies, installation instructions, and environment spec-
ifications are provided in the artifact repository.

          ARC divides cache into two lists: a one-hit list and a multi-
       hit list. A new object is first placed in the one-hit list and
       added to the multi-hit list on a second access. On a cache
       miss, ARC checks whether it has previously evicted the re-
       quested object by looking for it in the eviction history of both
       lists. If so, ARC expands that list’s size and correspondingly
       reduces the size of the other list. In this way, ARC adapts by
       dynamically adjusting the cache space partition to favor ei-
       ther 1) objects accessed only once recently (by expanding the
       one-hit list), or 2) objects accessed multiple times recently (by
       expanding the multi-hit list). CAR follows a similar design
       but notably replaces the LRU lists with FIFO queues.                          Figure 3: The average hit rate improvement over LRU for 8 repre-

                                                                                                                             This paper presents Merlin, an adaptive cache eviction algo-
Merlin uses the properties of FIFO queues to track objects
                                                                                                                             rithm that achieves high hit rates across diverse real-world
within an epoch (for hotness), as discussed in §5.2.
                                                                                                                             workloads. Merlin’s effectiveness stems from two key de-
   Therefore, to understand the sensitivity of epoch length,                                                                 signs. First, Merlin proposes a principled fine-grained access
we use the ghost queue size to approximate it. Specifically, a                                                               characterization method that also accounts for locality and
small ghost queue approximates a shorter epoch, as Merlin                                                                    cache size. Specifically, Merlin classifies objects into four
observes hotness for a smaller amount of time. Vice versa, a                                                                 types based on hotness and popularity, where the cache size
large ghost queue approximates a longer epoch. As shown                                                                      determines the thresholds, and the distribution of types re-
in Figure 16, varying ghost queue sizes has little impact,                                                                   flects the access patterns. Such a classification allows Merlin
suggesting that Merlin is robust to different epoch lengths.                                                                 to accurately capture a wide spectrum of access patterns be-
7.6                              Why is Merlin effective?                                                                    yond a few typical ones. Second, Merlin employs a unified
                                                                                                                             and cohesive architecture that cleanly separates component
To evaluate why Merlin is effective, we measure the preci-                                                                   responsibilities, thereby eliminating the interference seen
sion and average hit count of objects promoted from ghost                                                                    in prior designs. Evaluations on 11 datasets and 5,423 traces
queues across different adaptive algorithms. The precision                                                                   show that Merlin achieves high efficiency, scalability, and
is the fraction of promoted objects that are later accessed                                                                  low management overhead.
again, indicating the decision accuracy. The average hit count
captures how valuable these promoted objects actually are.                                                                   10                 Acknowledgment

Figure 4: Illustration of learning-augmented heuristics. (1) Offline pretraining (left): A foundation model is trained on a massive corpus of
trace features and optimal parameter labels to learn universal caching rules. (2) Online operation (right): The system decouples the critical
data path from the control path. The data path collects lightweight workload-level features, while the control path asynchronously queries the
pre-trained model to adapt the cache parameters to the current workload trace.

the heuristic’s parameters, an approach we call Learning-

We implement S4-FIFO in both libCacheSim for simulation-          strate that it incurs almost no overhead compared to heuristics.
based evaluation and Meta Cachelib for prototype evaluation

                                                                             In this section we present C LINK, an auto-sharded cache
                                                                             linked directly into application pods that scales to handle
                                                                             millions to billions of keys. It provides linearizable reads while
                                                                             remaining loosely coupled to storage. C LINK allows reads to
                                                                             access storage from any pod to preserve high availability, but
                                                                             only pods assigned the key may serve reads directly from their
                                                                             local cache. C LINK uses WriteGuards to avoid delayed writes
                                                                             and scales by operating on key ranges rather than individual
                                                                             keys. To ensure linearizable cached reads, C LINK maintains
                                                                             the following invariant:

10.2    Storage-layer caches
Many storage systems natively support automatic block
or row caching of popular tables and rows for fast
lookups [32, 45, 56, 69, 73–75, 86]. While such caches
provide linearizable reads, the storage layer quickly becomes
a performance bottleneck [88, 92, 93], causing practitioners
to explore solutions based on external caches.
10.3    Caches with weak read consistency
Many caches [11, 13, 16, 18, 23, 27, 28, 33, 40, 42, 48,
65, 71, 78, 87, 89, 92, 94] are based on TTLs, providing
eventually-consistent and not linearizable reads. Cache
invalidation [6, 22, 52, 67, 95, 97] has been explored. However,
none of these caches provide linearizable reads. TxCache [70]
provides transactional consistency for in process caches by
validating cached objects against a central database, but it dif-
fers from our approach in several key aspects. First, it does not
guarantee that reads return the latest committed value. Second,
it is not designed for auto-sharded or dynamically rebalanced
systems and therefore does not address correctness under
shifting key ownership. Third, it targets a single relational
database rather than a distributed, sharded storage layer.
11     Conclusion
This work introduced WriteGuards, a lightweight storage
mechanism that prevents delayed writes from previous owners
and enables loosely coupled caches to serve linearizable reads
from memory. Using this primitive, we presented C LINK, the
first in-process datacenter cache that provides linearizable
cached reads with low latency, and C RINK - R and C RINK - L,
two remote variants that offer the same guarantees for shared
and multi-tenant deployments. Our caches are performant:
C LINK reduces tail latency of reads by up to three orders
of magnitude. C RINK - R and C RINK - L also significantly cut

                                                                  2.2 Analysis of Existing DNN Inference on

                                                                  While many DNN inference frameworks exist for homoge-
                                                                  neous multi-core systems [37, 54] and heterogeneous SoCs

                                                                  formance constraints on AMP architectures. Their limita-
                                                                  tion stems from an implicit assumption of core symmetry
                                                                  in multi-threaded execution. This prevents the effective use
                                                                  of asymmetric cores and results in suboptimal performance.

                                                                    10    Conclusion
The same primitives carry over to the other studies: scal-
able hybrid execution (§ 8.7) treats QAC ’s cutting recipe          We introduce the hybrid tensor network (hTN) abstraction,
as an hEinsum, and error mitigation (§ 8.8) expresses QEM-          a unified framework that seamlessly integrates quantum and
routines as hTNs rather than separate library calls. Each           classical computation. hTNs address current hybrid com-
baseline is scoped to a single workload; composing them             puting limitations—programming fragmentation, static parti-
requires chaining tools, whereas qTPU expresses any work-           tioning, and poor scalability—through holistic representation
load, or arbitrary compositions, as one hTN (§ 8.9).                and optimization. Our system, qTPU, realizes hTNs through
                                                                    a declarative programming model, a compiler that balances
9      Related Work                                                 quantum error with classical cost, and an adaptable runtime
                                                                    for heterogeneous hybrid quantum-classical resources.

of quantum applications inherently rely on hybrid program-          mitigation demonstrates that qTPU achieves up to 53× faster
ming and execution models. Variational algorithms [27, 66],         compilation, 7.2× lower quantum error rate, 3,700× code re-
quantum machine learning [10, 51], quantum error mitiga-            duction, and 10,000× lower classical overhead than state-of-
tion [13, 20–22, 26, 65, 85, 86, 89, 98], and hybrid runtime sys-   the-art baselines. Through its concise, flexible, and scalable
tems [33,34,84,88,90] all interleave quantum circuit execution      abstraction for quantum-classical acceleration, qTPU enables
with classical optimization and/or postprocessing.                  automated and efficient heterogeneous resource utilization
   However, current approaches remain constrained by frag-          for next-generation quantum-enhanced applications.
mented programming models, a lack of holistic optimizations,

Hosting
The artifact is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/
nathanieltornow/qtpu (branch main). The exact version
evaluated by the AEC is tagged osdi26-ae. An archival snap-
shot with a citable DOI is mirrored on Zenodo.
Requirements
Software. Python 3.11–3.13 and uv (recommended) or pip.
The full dependency set is pinned in uv.lock and installable
via uv sync. A GPU-enabled Docker image is provided for
cuTensorNet comparisons (Fig. 12c).
Hardware. All non-hardware experiments run on a com-
modity x86_64 Linux or macOS workstation; 16 GB of RAM
is sufficient for the log-based plot regeneration, and 64 GB is
recommended to re-run the larger simulations from scratch.
An NVIDIA GPU with a recent CUDA toolchain is required
only to reproduce the cuTensorNet comparison in Fig. 12c.
IBM Quantum access. Fig. 11a (IBM Marrakesh) requires an
IBM Quantum account with access to the ibm_ marrakesh

                                                                   3.1    Threat Model
                                                                   Acumen assumes a threat model in which the relay server is
                                                                   actively malicious (functioning as the “network adversary”).
                                                                   Up to n−1 clients are compromised and deviate arbitrarily
                                                                   from the protocol. For example, malicious clients may engage
                                                                   in standard editing activities, such as inserting or deleting
                                                                   characters, but could also attempt more sophisticated attacks,
                                                                   such as sending inconsistent edits for the same document
                                                                   position to different clients.
                                                                     We assume the presence of a trusted public-key infras-

                    • Insertion operations o such that ∃od ∈ O, od targets o for deletion, and VVod ≤ (VVgc −1).
                    • Deletion operations od such that VVod ≤ (VVgc −1).
             2. Compute the set of CSTs: C = {n ∈ T | n is a tombstone ∧ ∃od ∈ O s.t. od deleted n ∧ VVod ≤ (VVgc −1)}
             3. Prune all leaf nodes in C. Repeat this step as needed if this generates new leaf CSTs.
             4. For each n ∈C such that n.parent ∈C, run the flatten subprocedure:
                    • Let p be n’s parent node, and let LC = n.left∥n.right be the concatenated child lists of n.
                    • Replace n in p’s left or right child list with the elements of LC .
             5. Let T ′ be the Treedoc object created as a result of Steps 3-4. Output (O′ ,T ′ ).

USENIX Association                            20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation                  2405
  We note that this protocol differs from our high-level
approach in that the set of snapshot operations at time VVu
is checked to be a subset of Ou , rather than full equality.
This is due to the aforementioned edit-history privacy (§5.2)
requirement that the sensitive data in operations in OS \ Ou
remain hidden. Snapdoc opts to directly withhold these
operations from the snapshot.
  This difference results in Snapdoc satisfying a weaker form
of snapshot consistency, where an attacker can produce a
valid snapshot comprised of any subset of the “true” state.
For instance, an attacker can issue a snapshot for a document
reading “AC” when it should be “ABC”. More formally, if SA
is the set of operations in a valid snapshot, then it is possible
to create a valid snapshot for any X ⊂ SA .
  Careful readers will notice that any user can locally
transform the document with an arbitrary set of operations
before creating a snapshot, such that the resulting document
is edited to the sender’s liking. The resulting snapshot is
technically valid, but the key difference to above attack is
that the sender edits are codified as operations and are visible
to the snapshot receiver. This satisfies Definition 1, since
these operations are part of a fork-causal consistent execution.
This contrasts with the Snapdoc attack, since the deletion of
operations is not caused by any operation in the execution.
For instance, suppose an honest user issued insertions to
create the word “TRAIN”. A malicious user could create
a snapshot consisting only of the honest user operations
deriving “RAN”, even though this state never appeared in
the global causal execution.
  Snapdoc requires new users to broadcast a noop operation
including their own state attestation. The new user will
then only accept messages that include the noop as a causal
dependency. If the user’s snapshot is malformed (in a
non-trivial way as to pass local verification), they will never
process honest user edits, nor will honest users process their
updates, as if they were on different causal forks.
  This satisfies the overall definition of fork-causal
consistency, but is still undesirable since the new user
cannot tell that their state is malformed without out-of-band
communication from an honest party.

                Mayur Akewar+           Dongsheng Luo+             Sandeep Madireddy∗          Janki Bhimani+
                                             + Florida International University
                                               ∗ Argonne National Laboratory




                         Abstract                                    1   Introduction
SMART attributes are the main telemetry for monitoring
Solid State Drives (SSDs) and predicting failures in large           SMART (Self Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technol-
fleets, but existing methods rely on heavy feature engineer-         ogy) attributes [2] are the primary telemetry for monitoring
ing and large supervised pipelines that must be retrained as         the health of Solid State Drives (SSDs) in production data-
hardware or workloads change and that compress rich tem-             centers [5, 7, 8, 17, 22–25, 30, 36, 38]. Each drive reports daily
poral behavior into opaque numeric scores. Large Language            counters such as reallocated sectors, pending sectors, and me-
Models (LLMs) offer structured reasoning and explanations,           dia errors that evolve over time. These long multivariate his-
yet perform poorly on raw SMART logs because the histo-              tories allow operators to identify at-risk drives before failure,
ries are long and multivariate, their temporal inductive bias        enabling proactive replacement and minimizing downtime.
is weak, and they hallucinate on numeric inputs. We present             A large body of work converts SMART logs into predictive
SMARTTalk, a new systems architecture that introduces a              models. Classical approaches use summary statistics and hand
representation layer for device telemetry. SMARTTalk con-            crafted temporal features fed into supervised learners such
verts each n day SMART window into a sequence of symbolic            as random forests and gradient boosted trees [7, 8, 10, 22, 37].
trend tokens that an LLM can reliably reason over. The sys-          Subsequent work introduces sequence models including au-
tem separates numerical trend extraction from language based         toencoders, LSTMs, and temporal convolutional networks to
reasoning through three stages. (1) It slices n-day SMART            capture richer temporal behavior [12,19,38]. Recent industrial

                                                                     4     Evaluation
                                                                     In this section, we evaluate SMARTTalk on real Alibaba
                                                                     SMART logs and study three questions. First, how well does
                                                                     it predict drive status compared with conventional SMART-
                                                                     based baselines and recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods?
                                                                     Second, how accurately can it predict time-to-failure (TTF)
                                                                     buckets? Third, how good are the generated explanations and
                                                                     recommendations, both in terms of automatic metrics and
                                                                     their alignment with desired actions?

2472    20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation                                      USENIX Association
Hook                                        Compatible?   Why
Native XDP [22, 31]                             ✓         The driver runs the program on an xdp_buff and expects a packet verdict. PeeR retains the packet as an xdp_frame on yield
                                                          and applies the verdict on resume, covering all five native actions. Multi-buffer and tail-call programs are rejected at load.
tc / TCX (direct-action) [16]                   ✓         The hook runs over an skb and returns a TC action. PeeR can apply terminal actions such as drop, stolen, and redirect
                                                          after a yield, once it retains the skb and the redirect state. Continuing actions re-enter the classifier chain or the network
                                                          stack, which lies outside the eBPF continuation, so PeeR supports only the terminal actions.
TC action chains (act_bpf) [15]                 ✗         An eBPF program is one action inside a larger action list. After it returns, the caller may run later actions, repeat, or jump to
                                                          another chain. Reconstructing this requires the full action-list and chain state, which the eBPF continuation does not capture.
XRP storage (NVMe) [56]                         ✓         The hook runs in NVMe completion on a request-scoped context and either completes the read or resubmits the next I/O.
                                                          PeeR can retain that request and resumption state across a yield and apply the action later. We do not implement this adapter,
                                                          but the contract fits the model.
Tracing, LSM, sockets, block [13, 14, 17]       ✗         These hooks fall outside PeeR’s model for two reasons. PeeR cannot defer the result for tracing or LSM: tracing runs
                                                          under locks held by the caller, and LSM must return its allow-or-deny decision before the caller continues. Socket and
                                                          process-context hooks already run preemptably and do not require deferral.

8.3.2      Instrumentation Overhead
                                                                                                             Existing mechanisms for deferred eBPF execution. Linux
The budget check the JIT inserts before each helper call is                                                  provides several mechanisms to defer eBPF work off the fast
PeeR’s only always-on cost, paid even by a program that never                                                path, such as eBPF timers [20], workqueues [21], and XDP’s
preempts. We measure it with an XDP program that calls                                                       cpumap redirect [50]. eBPF timers schedule callbacks for later,
bpf_get_prandom_u32 in a loop, comparing the stock JIT                                                       but they still run in softirq, steal time from interrupted appli-
against PeeR’s JIT with a budget set so the check executes                                                   cations, and lack hook context or I/O capabilities. Workqueues
on every call but never fires. The check adds one cycle per                                                  defer to a sleepable kernel worker, but each callback executes
helper call, and two when the scheduler is actively writing the                                              as a single eBPF invocation; the scheduler sees only the worker
per-CPU budget flag.                                                                                         thread, not individual eBPF tasks. cpumap queues packets to

with the prior study [37] that shows the scheduling subsystem     is able to determine whether the access is a load or a store.

to improve cacheline utilization, which rearranges the fields     than individual functions, we define fields of high affinity if

  together may result in false sharing.

and low operational efficiency. To address these challenges,          are typically stored and processed in separate infrastructures,

including logs, metrics, and traces. The key idea of DiTing           operational barriers for SREs but can also degrade perfor-

       shopping1          Open a shopping app and scroll down to browse products.
       shopping2          Open a shopping app, enter the “Me” page, and swipe.
       weather1           Open the weather app and send it to the background.
       weather2           Open the weather app and swipe left to switch cities.

The human-written Isabelle proof illustrates the procedural, tactic-driven reasoning style that is common in software verification.
We prompted two state-of-the-art LLMs, Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-5.1, to synthesize the same proof under controlled conditions,
with web search disabled to avoid any leakage of the original script. Although both models correctly recognized the proof
context and invoked some relevant tactics, neither succeeded in producing a valid proof even after roughly one minute of internal
reasoning. Their attempts frequently misuse the domain-specific wp tactic, or hallucinate nonexistent lemmas.

Figure 2: Overview of our neuro-symbolic proof-search framework. Starting from the initial proof state, the system repeatedly
generates candidate proof steps using a fine-tuned LLM, followed by rule-based symbolic revision to repair syntactic or semantic
issues in the proposed steps. Each accepted step is executed by Isabelle/HOL to derive new proof states, which are then filtered
by symbolic tools to prune states containing counterexamples or duplicates. The remaining states are ranked using cumulative
LLM log-probabilities, and the highest-scoring ones are selected for further expansion in a best-first search. If the search cannot
complete the proof, the framework finally invokes Sledgehammer to attempt to resolve the remaining goals.

7.4                  Summary and discussion                                                   A structural disadvantage of Spain is that, for the time being,

purpose (§1): it easily handled an array of natural benchmarks,                            constraints are more portable; they can be combined with
and we did not have to discard any benchmarks because Spain                                back-ends that provide different properties. Otti’s back-end,
lacked sufficient expressiveness.                                                          for example, provides zero-knowledge and non-interactivity.

   This reduction lowers the prover overhead versus natural                                enhanced properties.

 Setup: Prover P and Verifier V agree on the parameters of the protocol, which are as follows:
  • a small constant 𝜖 ≪ 1
  • an instance, X = ( 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶, in, out), consisting of rationals with unreduced denominator 𝐷 (a power of 2).
  • a polynomial commitment scheme PC satisfying Weak Integer Binding with parameters 𝑁max and 𝐷 max .
  • a large set of primes, 𝑃, from which V will sample in the protocol.
 Preprocessing: P and V performs the setup required by PC.
 Online phase: If at any point V’s check fails, it rejects.
  1. Using PC, P commits to a multilinear polynomial 𝑓˜ whose coefficients are purportedly integers. P sends this commitment to V.
         • Define 𝑤e := 𝑓˜/𝐷. Define 𝑤 as the coefficients of 𝑤
                                                              e, and define 𝑧 := (in, out, 1, 𝑤). If P is honest, then 𝑤 is chosen to make 𝑧 an
           𝜖-accurate assignment to X.
   2. P computes ∥𝐸 X,𝑧 ∥ 22 (over Q), and sends 𝑆 := ∥𝐸 X,𝑧 ∥ 22 · 𝐷 8 to V.
   3. V checks that 𝑆 is an integer, computes 𝐽 := 𝑆/𝐷 8 , and checks that 0 ≤ 𝐽 ≤ 𝜖 2 .
   4. V samples a random prime 𝑞 ∼ 𝑃, sends it to P, and P and V map all quantities in Q into F𝑞 via 𝜌𝑞 .
   5. V and P run a degree-4 sum-check primitive on

B    Artifact Appendix

Abstract
The artifact for RT packages the prototype checker, command
specifications, documentation, tests, benchmark inputs, and re-
production scripts used for the evaluation in §6. It is organized
to support three tasks: inspecting how the implementation re-
alizes the regular-type analysis described in the paper, running
functional checks for the core analyzer, and regenerating the
principal evaluation artifacts, including the accuracy sum-
maries, ablation and false-result breakdowns, bug-detection
comparison, timing table, and automata-size plots.

Scope
The artifact supports the paper’s design and evaluation claims.
In particular, it covers: (1) the RT implementation of regu-
lar stream and command types from §3, the type-checking
procedure in §3.3, and the regular-language operators and
FST machinery from §4; (2) the configurable mechanisms in
§5, including environment concretization, annotations, and
heuristics; (3) the motivating example and the seven bench-
mark sets discussed in §2 and §6; and (4) the automation for
reproducing the main tables and figures reported in §6.

Contents
The artifact includes the following components:
 • the RT checker implementation and command type
   database;
 • support code for regular-language operations, finite-state
   transducers, annotations, concretization, and heuristics;
 • documentation, including the top-level README and
   artifact-evaluation instructions;

 • functional tests and smoke-test examples, including the
   motivating example from §2;
 • the benchmark suites used in the paper’s evaluation and
   the configuration needed to run baseline comparisons
   against ShellCheck and LADDERT YPES; and

 • scripts for checking the artifact, reproducing the full eval-
   uation, and generating the resulting tables and plots.

Hosting
The artifact is publicly available as a GitHub repository at
https://github.com/atlas-brown/rt.
